{"id":27,"title":"Split roster into agent_tools (configs) + processes (instances) to match Solo's two-layer model","body":"Follow-up to #16. Today the `roster` table is a hybrid: each row is both a config (name, command, cwd) and the implicit single instance of it. Liveness is derived from Zellij pane state, not stored. This can't represent Solo's normal case of N instances per config (e.g. two Claude processes both spawned from agent tool #3) and leaves no way to numerically address a specific running instance.

## Direction (from discussion 2026-05-23)

Adopt Solo's two-layer model, but keep PANopt's per-project scoping and unified-namespace properties:

- **agent_tools** (new table) - durable configurations.
  - Columns: `id`, `project_id`, `name`, `command`, `tool_type`, `enabled`, timestamps.
  - Per-project for now (Solo's tools are global; PANopt can revisit if cross-project sharing becomes useful).
  - Ids allocated from `projects.next_id` (the unified sequence from #16).

- **processes** (rename/expand the existing `roster` table) - per-project instances.
  - Columns: `id`, `project_id`, `kind` (agent / command / terminal), `name`, plus `agent_tool_id` FK when `kind='agent'`.
  - Until PANopt owns spawn lifecycle, the row can mirror Zellij pane state on a best-effort basis; once lifecycle is owned (DESIGN.md S10), this table holds pid, status, last-seen, idle/thinking, etc.
  - Ids allocated from `projects.next_id` (same unified sequence).

Net effect: both layers participate in the global `#N` namespace, so "agent 54" resolves to whichever row carries id 54 - config or instance - unambiguously.

## Why not just expand roster

`roster` mixes "what to run" with "what's running." Splitting cleanly mirrors Solo, lets one config back many instances (Solo proves the value), and keeps DESIGN.md S6.6's distinction explicit ("the durable set of processes the project is configured to run" vs. live state) instead of leaving it implicit.

## Migration

- New schema version (V6).
- Move `kind='agent'` rows from `roster` to `agent_tools` (configs).
- Move `kind='command'` and `kind='terminal'` rows to `processes` (instances - the only existing PANopt rows of those kinds were always instances, since there was no separate config layer).
- Existing roster ids are preserved across the move (still unique under the unified `next_id`, so no remapping needed).
- Drop the old `roster` table.

For agents that declared a stable identity via `?agent=<id>` it's wrong: the user introduced a name (`gregz-main`, `agent-4dc2f9df`), and that name shouldn't decay just because the agent is between tool calls.

The 5-min → 30-min bump (state.rs:30) is a band-aid, not a fix — any conversation gap longer than the threshold reproduces it.

## Why not connection-based presence

The naive answer is "use MCP session lifecycle, or TCP socket open/close, as the presence signal". Both would be real, no idle guesswork. They don't work in practice because Claude Code's HTTP MCP client opens a session per tool call, initializes, calls, and tears down within ~30ms. Daemon log confirms this — sessions are continuously created and closed. "Present while a session is open" would mean every agent flickers in and out many times per minute; "present once initialize has been seen" never times out without re-introducing idle-prune. The MCP spec lets clients choose persistent SSE or one-shot POSTs; we don't get to dictate Claude Code's choice.

## Model

Declared identity, layered with two opt-in signals.

- **Declared identity (core).** A stable `?agent=` key stays in the registry until the daemon restarts. Carries `last_seen` for UI staleness annotation, but presence does not gate on it. Session-id keys still idle-prune as today — those are real throwaway entries.
- **Cooperative `disconnect` tool.** Any agent that wants to leave cleanly calls it. The daemon removes the entry and releases its locks immediately. For hand-launched agents this is the only way to leave cleanly short of a daemon restart.
- **Launcher hook (connection-based, where we can get it).** The cockpit already detects pane death (close-gate uses it). The launcher calls `disconnect` on behalf of the pane's agent so cockpit-spawned agents get real connection-based presence without the agent itself caring. This is the OS-level signal we *can* observe, because the process is one the launcher spawned.

Net result: accurate-when-the-launcher-knows (cockpit), best-effort-when-cooperative (everywhere), graceful-degradation-when-neither (last_seen annotation in the UI).

Not duplicates. They live on two different planes of "the agent model," and they barely touch the same files. Here's the breakdown:

## #27 — durable data-model split (config vs. instance)
This is about the **persisted SQLite layer**. Today the `roster` table is a hybrid row that's both *config* (name, command, cwd) and the *single implicit instance* of it. #27 splits that into:
- `agent_tools` — durable configs ("what to run")
- `processes` — instances ("what's running"), with an `agent_tool_id` FK

It's a schema migration (V6), a `roster_* → agent_tool_* / process_*` MCP rename, projection-path changes, DESIGN.md §6.6. Touches `db.rs`, `model.rs`, `state.rs`, `handler.rs`, projection.

## #83 — live-presence model (declared identity vs. activity sample)
This is about the **in-memory registry** — the volatile thing that answers `agent_list`. The bug: every agent is pruned after `AGENT_MAX_IDLE` (`state.rs:30`), which is correct for throwaway session-id keys but wrong for agents that declared a stable `?agent=` identity. The fix is declared-identity persistence + a cooperative `agent_leave`/disconnect + a launcher pane-death hook. | | #27 | #83 |
|---|---|---|
| Plane | durable SQLite (`agent_tools` + `processes`) | in-memory registry |
| Concern | *modeling* one config → N instances | *presence/liveness* of connected agents |
| Trigger | Solo's two-layer model; `#N` addressability | agents not seeing each other across idle gaps |
| Core file | `db.rs` / `model.rs` | `registry.rs` |

You could do either without the other.

Neither todo references the other, so whoever implements the second one could accidentally re-invent the first's last_seen concept.

### 6.6 Agent tools and processes

PANopt splits a project's launchable agents and commands across two tables, a
config layer and an instance layer, mirroring Solo's two-layer model:

- **`agent_tools`** - durable per-project configurations: name, command, cwd,
  a free-form `tool_type`, and an `enabled` flag controlling whether the
  config is offered in spawn UIs. One tool can back many running instances.
- **`processes`** - per-project instances of an agent, command, or terminal:
  `kind` (`agent` / `command` / `terminal`), name, command, cwd, an optional
  `agent_tool_id` back-reference, plus nullable lifecycle columns (`pid`,
  `status`, `agent_state`, `last_seen`) reserved for a future follow-up that
  owns spawn lifecycle.

The split lets a project carry two Claude instances both spawned from agent
tool `#3`, with each instance addressable by its own `#N`. When a process is
spawned from a tool, the tool's `command` and `cwd` are copied into the
process row so post-spawn edits to the tool don't perturb the running
instance. Deleting a tool nulls the `agent_tool_id` back-reference on any
process that referenced it; the live instance keeps running.

Both tables draw ids from the unified per-project `next_id` counter
(Section 6.4), so a `#N` reference still resolves to exactly one row across
todos, notes, agent_tools, and processes.

Whether a process is currently running is *not* stored today: the cockpit
derives it from live Zellij pane state, same as the pre-V6 roster did. The
nullable lifecycle columns turn that into a follow-up rather than a schema
break, once panoptd owns process spawn (Section 10).

The config and instance layers each project to their own markdown file:
`.panopt/agent_tools.md` and `.panopt/processes.md`. The cockpit sidebar
currently renders only `processes.md`, because it is a live-state view;
agent_tools render once a spawn UI lands.

Both layers are distinct from the agent registry (Section 6.3): the registry
is the ephemeral set of MCP agents *currently connected*, while agent_tools
and processes are the durable set of agents/commands/terminals the project
is configured to run and the live instances of them.

Good instinct — there are three levels, and the third (types) is the genuinely new one. #27 only ever built two (`agent_tools` + `processes`). Let me map your three onto what exists and then take on the 1:1 question head-on, because that's the crux.

## The three levels, mapped

| Your level | What it holds | Scope | Status today |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Agent type** (claude-code, codex, pi, opencode) | how to *interop*: launch command shape, identity injection (`PANOPT_AGENT`/token env), TUI status parsing, pane-death detection, prompt format | global / shared | **doesn't exist** — §6.6 has only a free-form `tool_type` string |
| **Agent config** (a slot in the agents pane) | references a type; name, cwd, command overrides, system prompt, `enabled` | per-project, durable | exists as `agent_tools` (#27) |
| **Agent instance** (the running agent) | references a config; `pid`, `status`, `agent_state`, `last_seen`, session | per-project, ephemeral | exists as `processes` with those columns *reserved but unused* (#27/§6.6) |

So the type layer is a clean new tier *above* what #27 built — not a reshuffle of it.

## Agent type: code, not a table

One thing to settle early: the type level carries **behavior** (how to launch claude-code vs codex, how to parse "thinking" out of each one's TUI). Behavior lives in code — a trait/adapter registry keyed by `claude-code` / `codex` / `opencode`, not DB rows. A `agent_types` table would just be a denormalized cache of what the code already has to know. So: elevate §6.6's free-form `tool_type` from "any string" to "a key into the adapter registry." Add a thin per-type-defaults table later only if users need to tweak defaults — but the source of truth is the adapter. This keeps the type level from becoming fake data.

## The real question: collapse config and instance at 1:1?

The 1:1 you're seeing is **a policy you'd be imposing**, not an inherent property. #27 exists *because* Solo is N:1 ("two Claude instances both spawned from agent tool #3"). So the honest framing isn't "they map 1:1, why two tables" — it's "I'm choosing to forbid N:1; given that, do I still want two."

Even under a hard 1:1, a config and an instance are not the same thing — they're **desired state vs. running state** (spec vs. status, à la Kubernetes):

- Config = *what you want*: "a reviewer slot, claude-code, this cwd, enabled."
- Instance = *what's happening*: "pid 4821, thinking, last seen 12s ago."

These legitimately **diverge even at 1:1**:
- You edit the config while it's running → config changed, instance still on old params until restart. (§6.6 already bakes this in: command/cwd are *copied* into the process row on spawn precisely so edits don't perturb a live instance.)
- Config `enabled` but the instance crashed → slot exists, nothing running.
- Config exists, never started → instance is null.

A merged single-row "slot" with nullable runtime columns *can* model this — but it muddies "edit the slot" (are you editing desired or live?) and it forces every consumer to know which columns are meaningful when stopped.

**The decisive test: does anything need to attach to a *run* rather than the *slot*?** Look at the backlog:
- #113 — "associate agent **session(s)** with todo" (plural, per-run)
- #105 — "store agent **plans** as first-class object"

A plan and a session belong to a *run*, not to the durable slot. If the reviewer slot runs today and again next week, those are different sessions with different plans — linking them to the config would be wrong. That alone says instances need their own identity that comes and goes while the config persists. Merge them and you can't say "the previous run."

### Recommendation

**Keep config and instance as separate concepts (and rows), but collapse them in the *UI*.** The 1:1 makes the sidebar trivial — one row per config, with a status badge and a start/stop toggle; the instance lives "inside" the slot visually. So the split costs you nothing in UI complexity, and it buys you:
- clean desired/actual divergence (the spec/status property #27 already half-built),
- run-level identity for sessions/plans/todos (#113, #105),
- the N:1 door stays open at ~zero cost (it's the same schema #27 shipped — you'd just relax a uniqueness constraint later).

The cost is one join you always do. That's cheap.

**Counter-position, stated fairly:** if you're confident you'll *never* want run history or N:1, then merging into a single slot table with nullable runtime columns is genuinely simpler, and you shouldn't carry a table you don't use. But #113/#105 are already on the board signaling you *do* want run-level attachment — so I lean split.

Refining your three into four, in dependency order:

1. **Agent-type adapter layer (code).** Define the trait/registry; ship with `claude-code` as the only entry. Everything references it, so it's first. (Can be a hardcoded constant initially.)
2. **Finish config + instance plumbing.** Mostly *done* by #27 — what's left: make `tool_type` reference the adapter registry, and lock in the spec/status story (which fields are desired vs. runtime). Small.
3. **Config form** (create/edit slots). The §6.6 "agent_tools render once a spawn UI lands" piece — a CRUD form mirroring TodoForm/ScratchpadForm.
4. **Instance lifecycle UI** (start/stop/report). Populate the reserved `processes` columns, panoptd owns spawn (§10), sidebar shows live status. **Absorbs #111** (which is only the render half). Biggest, last.

Clean chain: 1 → 2 → 3, and 1 → 2 → 4. 3 and 4 are independent of each other (you can edit configs before lifecycle works, and vice versa).

If you buy this, the encoding is: add a new todo for (1) the type layer, re-scope #27 to (2), add a todo for (3) the config form, and add a lifecycle todo for (4) that absorbs #111 and links #27/#83/#105/#113. You're right, and my "denormalized cache" line was wrong. It's only true for the *control flow*. The moment you look at the actual contents of a type, a big chunk of it is data that (a) drifts on someone else's release schedule and (b) is environment-specific — neither of which belongs compiled into the panopt binary. The clean model isn't "code vs. data," it's the **device-driver model: a thin driver (code) + a profile (runtime data) per type.**

## Decompose what a "type" actually owns

| Responsibility | claude-code example | Code or data? |
|---|---|---|
| **Launch mechanism** (how MCP gets wired: env vs config-file vs flag) | `claude --mcp-config <json>` + `PANOPT_*` env | **code** — a small enum of mechanisms |
| **argv template / flags** | the exact flag names, model arg | **data** — strings that change when the CLI changes |
| **Binary path / how to find it** | `claude` vs `/opt/.../claude` vs a version pin | **data** — *machine* fact, can't be compiled in |
| **Identity injection values** | `PANOPT_AGENT`, `PANOPT_NAME`, `PANOPT_TOKEN` names | **data** (the var *names*); **code** (that it's env vs a file) |
| **Status parsing — source** | screen-scrape the TUI vs read a JSON side-channel | **code** — different source of truth |
| **Status parsing — patterns** | the regex/strings for "thinking / waiting / done" | **data** — and the *most* drift-prone of all |
| **Default model / args / system-prompt scaffold** | seeds a new config | **data** |
| **Pane-death / health detection** | the mechanism | **code**; thresholds **data** |

The control flow — *how* you assemble an MCP config, *whether* status comes from a TUI or a socket — is genuinely code. Everything that's a *value plugged into that flow* is data. My mistake was collapsing the two.

## Three forces that make type-level runtime config unavoidable

1. **Drift on an upstream cadence you don't control.** When Claude Code changes its spinner text or Codex renames a flag, your status-parse patterns and argv break. If those live in the binary, every upstream UI tweak forces a panopt rebuild + release. As data (shipped defaults, user-overridable), you patch a profile, not recompile. This is the strongest argument and it's exactly your intuition.

2. **Machine/user-specificity.** Binary path, which version is installed, auth method — these aren't even "defaults," they're environment facts that vary per machine. There is no compiled-in value for "where is `claude` on *this* box."

3. **Extensibility without a PR.** Someone wants `opencode` or a homegrown agent. If type = code, they fork panopt. If type = generic driver + profile, the long tail of "spawn a TUI, inject env, match these strings" is *data-only* — a generic adapter parameterized by a profile row. Only structurally novel agents (non-TUI, different MCP wiring) need bespoke code.

## So the line, precisely

The test for "new agent type = code or config?": **does it need new control flow, or just new values?**
- New values into existing flow (different argv, different binary, different status regexes) → **profile row, no code.** This should be the common case.
- New control flow (parse a fundamentally different output format, wire MCP a structurally different way) → **new driver impl.** The exception.

The aspiration: a single `GenericAgentDriver` covers most types, and the registry is *mostly* profile rows pointing at it; bespoke drivers are the minority.

## Where the profile data lives

It's layered, and it's **global scope, not per-project** (distinct from the per-project `agent_tools`):

```
shipped defaults (versioned file in the repo — claude-code's status patterns ship here)
   ▲ overridden by
machine/user config (binary paths, installed version, auth)
   ▲ overridden by
config-level fields (model, args) — these are per-project and already live at level 2
```

Project-specific tweaks don't belong at the type level — they're what level-2 configs already override (command/cwd/model). So the type profile stays global: shipped defaults merged with machine-local overrides. Table-vs-file is a downstream packaging call (a file is fine for power-user regex edits; a table if you want a sidebar form for it) — the *layered merge* is the real structure.

## Net effect on the model

Level 1 changes from "code" to **driver + profile**:
- §6.6's free-form `tool_type` string becomes a **key into a type registry**.
- A registry entry = `{ driver: Generic | Bespoke<X> (code), profile: merged data }`.
- Most entries are `Generic + profile`.

Levels 2 and 3 are unchanged from the last message (config slot → instance, kept separate for the spec/status + run-identity reasons).

This sharpens the ordering's step 1 from "hardcode an adapter" to "define the driver trait **and** the profile schema + shipped-defaults file, with claude-code as one generic-driver profile." Want me to fold this into the model and lay out the four todos now, or keep pressure-testing — e.g. the table-vs-file decision for the profile, or whether the generic driver can really cover status-parsing without per-agent code?

## Launch as a spawn-spec template (data)

A launch is: given facts panopt can supply — `{agent_id, name, token, mcp_url, project_path, cwd, model, …}` — produce `(argv, env, files-to-materialize)`. All three "mechanisms" are just *where a placeholder lands*:

- **flag** → placeholder goes in `argv`
- **env** → placeholder goes in the `env` map
- **config-file** → render a template to a temp file, put its path in `argv`

That's one generic substitution engine over a profile. Two types, same interpreter, different data:

```yaml
# claude-code
spawn:
  argv: ["claude", "--mcp-config", "{{file:mcp_config}}"]
  env:  {}
  files:
    mcp_config: |
      { "mcpServers": { "panopt": { "url": "{{mcp_url}}",
        "headers": {"Authorization": "Bearer {{token}}"} } } }   # identity via file

# codex (hypothetical)
spawn:
  argv: ["codex", "--server", "{{mcp_url}}", "--token", "{{token}}"]   # identity via flags
  env:  { "CODEX_SESSION": "{{agent_id}}" }                            # ...and env
  files: {}
```

No per-type code there. And no new security boundary — `agent_tools` already stores a free-form `command` (#27), and you spawn `argv` directly (a list, no shell parse), so escaping is largely moot.

## The principle, applied consistently

The code/data line isn't "mechanism vs. values." It's: **does a generic interpreter exist for this?** If yes, the per-type part is *all data*. Code is the interpreter; data is the program it runs. That's true for launch (template substitution) exactly as it is for status (pattern match). I applied it to status but not launch — your call corrects that.

## So what's irreducibly code, after this

Two things, both **fixed and generic — never per-type**:

1. **The interpreters**: the substitution engine (launch), the pattern engine (status), the pane-death/health probe. One each.
2. **The placeholder providers**: the code that *produces* the facts to inject — `agent_id`, the bearer `token`, the `mcp_url`. Panopt has to compute these; that's not data. But it's one shared set, not per-agent.

Per-type code drops to a single rare case: an agent that needs a **new kind of step** the interpreters can't express — e.g., status only knowable by polling an HTTP endpoint, or a launch that must spawn, wait for a port, then POST a config. And the moment you add that step *kind* to an interpreter, it becomes declarable data for everyone after. So even the escape hatch is self-eliminating over time.

## Net effect

The "driver + profile" framing collapses further: there's effectively **one generic agent runner with a fixed library of interpreters, and a *type is purely a profile (data)*.** Code grows only when you discover a new step *kind* — few, and reusable once added. `tool_type` becomes a key into a table of profiles, full stop; the "registry of drivers" I posited mostly evaporates.

This makes step 1 of the ordering even lighter: not "define a driver trait," but **"define the spawn-spec + status-profile schema and the generic interpreters, ship claude-code as the first profile row."** No claude-code-specific code at all if it fits the template — which, from the sketch above, it does.

Umbrella for refining the agent model into three explicit levels, converged in design discussion 2026-05-31. Tracks the child todos tagged `agent-model`.

## The three levels

1. **Agent types = data (profiles), not code.** A type is a *profile row* that drives a fixed set of generic interpreters; `tool_type` becomes a key into a profile registry. There is no per-type code in the common case.
   - **Launch is data**: a spawn-spec template — `argv` template + `env` map + `files`-to-materialize — over a fixed placeholder set (`{agent_id, name, token, mcp_url, project_path, cwd, model, …}`). env-vs-flag-vs-config-file are just *where a placeholder lands*, not different mechanisms. One substitution engine, not a branch per type.
   - **Status is data**: pattern rules (`thinking/idle/waiting/done`) over agent output, run by one generic pattern engine.
   - **Irreducibly code** (fixed, generic, never per-type): the interpreters (substitution, pattern, health/pane-death) and the placeholder providers (the code that produces `token`/`mcp_url`/`agent_id`). New per-type code is needed only for a genuinely new *step kind* the interpreters can't express — rare, and reusable as data once added.
   - **Scope**: global, layered — shipped-defaults file ← machine/user overrides. Distinct from per-project `agent_tools`.

2. **Agent configs = per-project durable slots** (`agent_tools`, shipped in #27). Reference a type; hold name, cwd, command/arg overrides, system prompt, `enabled`. A slot is a lifecycle-managed line in the project's agents pane.

3. **Agent instances = per-project ephemeral runs** (`processes`, shipped in #27 with reserved `pid/status/agent_state/last_seen`). Reference a config; one per config (1:1 policy, N:1 door left open). Born on start, die on stop.

## Why config and instance stay separate even at 1:1
They are *desired state vs. running state* (spec/status): config = what you want, instance = what's happening, and they legitimately diverge (edited-but-not-restarted, crashed, never-started). Decisively, run-level identity is needed so **sessions (#113) and plans (#105) attach to a run, not the durable slot**. The 1:1 keeps the *UI* one-row-per-slot regardless.

## Relationship to existing todos
- #27 (config/instance schema split) — **schema + MCP surface shipped**; remaining wiring lives in the `tool_type → profile` child. Recommend verifying and closing #27.
- #83 (declared-identity registry) — the registry is the *runtime presence* of an instance; the liveness child must consume it, not re-model liveness.
- #111 (monitor agent status in pane) — **absorbed** by the lifecycle-UI child.
- #105 (plans), #113 (sessions) — downstream consumers; this work gives them a run to attach to.

input.body:
Foundation for the type level. Define the **type-profile** data model and load it; no spawning or parsing yet.

## Scope
- Schema for a profile: spawn-spec (`argv` template, `env` map, `files` to materialize) + status rules (patterns → `thinking/idle/waiting/done`) + metadata (`tool_type` key, display name, default model/args).
- Shipped-defaults file in the repo (versioned, code-reviewed), with **claude-code** as the first profile.
- Layered merge: shipped-defaults ← machine/user override file. Global scope (not per-project), distinct from `agent_tools`.
- Loader returns the merged profile set, keyed by `tool_type`.

## Acceptance
- Loading yields a merged claude-code profile; a machine override changes a field (e.g. binary path) and the merge reflects it.
- Profile set is addressable by `tool_type` key.
- No spawn/parse logic here — pure data + load.

Blocks the spawn interpreter, status interpreter, and `tool_type` wiring. Part of EPIC (agent-model). DESIGN: new §6.7.

input.title: Agent types: spawn-spec interpreter + placeholder providers
input.body:
The launch half of the type interpreters. A pure engine: profile spawn-spec + injected facts → a concrete `(argv, env, files)` spawn plan.

## Scope
- Template substitution over the spawn-spec: resolve `{{placeholder}}` (and `{{file:NAME}}`) in `argv`, `env`, and `files`.
- **Placeholder providers** (the one piece of real, generic code): produce the injectable facts — `agent_id`, `name`, `token`, `mcp_url`, `project_path`, `cwd`, `model`. Reuse the existing identity/token machinery (`agent-config`).
- Materialize `files` to temp paths and back-substitute their paths into `argv`/`env`.
- Spawn argv directly (no shell) — list form, so no shell-escaping surface.

## Acceptance
- Given the claude-code profile + a project/identity, produces the exact argv/env/temp-file the cockpit would otherwise hand-build.
- A second profile shape (env-based + flag-based identity) renders correctly from the same engine — proves no per-type branch.
- Pure/unit-tested; no actual process spawn here (that's the lifecycle child).

Blocked by the profile schema child. Feeds the spawn/kill child. Part of EPIC (agent-model).

input.title: Agent types: status pattern interpreter
input.body:
The status half of the type interpreters. A pure engine: profile status rules + agent output snapshot → derived `agent_state` (`thinking/idle/waiting/done`).

## Scope
- Generic pattern engine evaluating a profile's status rules against captured agent output.
- Define the output source contract (TUI snapshot / log tail) the engine consumes — abstract over *where* the bytes come from so the lifecycle child can wire the real source.
- Fixture-driven: ship sample claude-code output snippets and assert the derived state.

## Acceptance
- Claude-code fixtures classify into the right `agent_state`.
- Adding a new state pattern is a profile edit, not code.
- Pure/unit-tested; not yet wired to a live process (that's the liveness child).

Note: this is the engine; consuming it to populate `processes.agent_state` + reconciling with the #83 registry happens in the liveness child. Blocked by the profile schema child. Part of EPIC (agent-model).

input.title: Configs/instances: wire tool_type → profile registry + formalize spec/status split
input.body:
Connect the existing `agent_tools`/`processes` tables (shipped in #27) to the new type level, and lock the desired-vs-running column semantics.

## Scope
- `agent_tools.tool_type` becomes a **key into the profile registry** (validate on create/update that it names a known profile; reject unknown).
- Formalize the spec/status split on `processes`: document which columns are *desired* (copied-from-config at spawn) vs *runtime* (`pid/status/agent_state/last_seen`), and which are null when stopped.
- No new tables — #27 already built these. This is the reference + semantics layer.

## Acceptance
- Creating an `agent_tool` with an unknown `tool_type` is rejected; a known one succeeds.
- DESIGN §6.6 updated to state the spec/status semantics and the profile reference.

Follows #27 (recommend verifying #27's schema shipped and closing it). Blocked by the profile schema child. Blocks the config UI and the spawn/kill child. Part of EPIC (agent-model).

input.title: Agent config management UI: list + create/edit form
input.body:
The config (slot) management surface in the cockpit — the §6.6 "agent_tools render once a spawn UI lands" piece.

## Scope
- Render `agent_tools` in the sidebar (currently only `processes.md` renders).
- CRUD form mirroring TodoForm/ScratchpadForm: pick a **type** (dropdown from the profile registry), set name, cwd, command/arg overrides, system prompt, `enabled`.
- Wire to the existing `agent_tool_create/update/delete` MCP tools.
- Inherit the form-refresh-while-open behavior (mirror #40/#65).

## Acceptance
- Can create, edit, and delete an agent config slot from the cockpit.
- Type dropdown is populated from loaded profiles; an invalid type can't be submitted.
- Sidebar lists configs distinctly from running processes.

Blocked by the tool_type→profile wiring child. Independent of the lifecycle children (you can manage configs before start/stop works). Part of EPIC (agent-model).

input.title: Instance lifecycle: panoptd owns spawn / kill
input.body:
The core of DESIGN §10 lifecycle ownership: panoptd starts and stops instances instead of liveness being derived from Zellij pane state.

## Scope
- `process_start(config)`: resolve the spawn plan via the spawn-spec interpreter, materialize files, spawn the process, write a `processes` row with `pid`/`status` (copy config's command/cwd into the row per §6.6 copy-on-spawn).
- `process_stop(#N)`: terminate the instance, clear/flip runtime columns.
- Decide spawn host: panoptd directly vs. via the cockpit/Zellij pane (the launcher already spawns panes — keep panes as the host, panoptd records/owns the lifecycle record). Resolve this explicitly.
- 1:1 policy: starting a config that already has a live instance is a no-op/focus, not a second spawn (N:1 door left closed for now).

## Acceptance
- Starting a config produces a running process and a `processes` row with a live pid/status; stopping it terminates and updates the row.
- Spawn plan matches what the cockpit previously hand-built (no behavior regression for claude-code panes).

Blocked by the spawn interpreter child and the tool_type→profile wiring child. Blocks liveness reporting and the lifecycle UI. Gives #105/#113 a run to attach to. Part of EPIC (agent-model). DESIGN §10.

input.title: Instance lifecycle: liveness + status reporting (reconcile with registry)
input.body:
Populate the runtime columns on `processes` from real signals, resolving the #83 seam so liveness is modeled once.

## Scope
- Wire the status pattern interpreter to a live output source for each running instance; write `agent_state`/`last_seen`.
- Reconcile signal sources: registry presence (#83), pane/process liveness, and status patterns. Decide the authority — e.g. process-alive from the spawn child, presence/last_seen cross-checked against the #83 registry, fine-grained `agent_state` from the pattern engine. The registry is the *runtime presence of a `processes` row*, not a parallel model.
- Project the live state to `.panopt/processes.md`.

## Acceptance
- A running instance shows correct `status` + `agent_state` that tracks the agent's real activity.
- Registry and `processes` agree on presence — no double source of truth for "is it alive."

Blocked by the status interpreter child and the spawn/kill child. Relates to #83. Blocks the lifecycle UI. Part of EPIC (agent-model). DESIGN §6.3/§6.6.

input.title: Instance lifecycle UI: start/stop controls + status badges
